entry: Generalized belief about a category of people, studied in [[Social psychology|social psychology]]. Stereotypes concern a group's personality, preferences, appearance or abilities, and they simplify information processing by letting people rely on stored knowledge rather than new input. They are often faulty and resistant to new information. Research on their accuracy has yielded mixed results: studies of national-origin and astrological-sign stereotypes found them inaccurate, while studies of gender stereotypes found them more likely to reflect reality. Explicit stereotypes are conscious beliefs that people knowingly use to judge others, whereas implicit stereotypes are automatic, involuntary associations between a social group and a domain or attribute. Stereotypes are regarded as the most cognitive component of intergroup attitudes, often occurring without conscious awareness; [[Prejudice|prejudice]] is the affective component, and discrimination the behavioral one. Stereotypes, prejudice, [[Racism|racism]], and discrimination are related but distinct concepts.

Medical procedure that intentionally and permanently leaves a person unable to reproduce. Sterilization comprises several methods of permanent [[Birth control|birth control]] available to both sexes, and reversal is generally difficult. The most common are tubal ligation (salpingectomy) for women and vasectomy for men. Tubal sterilization is highly effective, and surgical complications are low in the [[United States]], but it remains [[Surgery|surgery]] with risks, and women have a higher risk of serious side effects than men who have a vasectomy. Some studies estimate that 3% of women become [[Pregnancy|pregnant]] after tubal ligation; if this happens, the risk of ectopic gestation is high. Sterilization may be voluntary or promoted by governments, and some governments have historically or presently run compulsory or incentivized programs, while certain nations restrict or prohibit the practice.

[[Organic compound|Organic compound]] with four fused rings, designated A, B, C and D. Steroids have two principal biological functions: as components of [[Cell membrane|cell membranes]], where they alter membrane fluidity, and as signaling molecules. Examples include the [[Lipid|lipid]] [[Cholesterol|cholesterol]], the sex hormones estradiol and [[Testosterone|testosterone]], anabolic steroids, and the anti-inflammatory corticosteroid dexamethasone. Hundreds occur in fungi, plants and animals, and all are manufactured in cells from sterol precursors. The name derives from cholesterol, a sterol first described in gallstones, and the steroid nucleus typically has seventeen carbon atoms in four fused rings. Cutting ring B produces secosteroids, one of which is vitamin D3. Widely used trivial names of natural steroids with significant biologic activity include progesterone, testosterone and cortisol.

Medical device for listening to sounds inside the body, used in auscultation. A stethoscope has a small disc-shaped resonator placed against the skin, with one or two tubes leading to earpieces. It is used to listen to the heart, lungs and intestines and to blood flow in arteries and veins, and it is commonly used with a sphygmomanometer when measuring [[Blood pressure|blood pressure]]. René Laennec invented the first stethoscope in [[France]] in 1816, a wooden monaural tube that spared him from placing his ear directly on a woman's chest. Arthur Leared invented a binaural version in 1851, and George Philip Cammann perfected a binaural design for commercial production the following year. A design by Rappaport and Sprague in the 1940s became the standard by which other stethoscopes are measured.

American businessman and investor. Ballmer was hired at [[Microsoft]] by [[Bill Gates]] in 1980 and served as [[Chief executive officer|chief executive officer]] of the company from 2000 to 2014. Under his leadership Microsoft tripled sales and doubled profits, but it lost its market dominance and missed the ascendance of smartphones. He owns the Los Angeles Clippers of the [[National Basketball Association]] and co-founded the Ballmer Group, a philanthropic investment company.

American media executive and political strategist. Bannon ran the 2016 presidential campaign of [[Donald Trump]] as [[Chief executive officer|chief executive officer]] and then served as White House chief strategist until Trump fired him. A former investment banker at [[Goldman Sachs]], he co-founded Breitbart News and was its executive chairman. In 2022 he was convicted of contempt of Congress for refusing a subpoena from the January 6 House select committee, and in 2025 he pleaded guilty to New York state fraud charges linked to a border-wall fundraising campaign.

South African anti-apartheid activist and leader of the Black Consciousness Movement, which sought the psychological empowerment of black people. Biko helped found the South African Students' Organisation, which he believed black people had to lead independently of white liberals, and he was influenced by the Martinican philosopher [[Frantz Fanon]]. He popularized the slogan "black is beautiful" and helped found the Black People's Convention in 1972. The government placed him under a banning order in 1973, and he was detained several times. He died in police custody after his arrest; the official inquest attributed his injuries to a fall, though forensic evidence indicated assault. He is regarded as one of the earliest icons of the movement against [[Apartheid|apartheid]].

American actor and comedian. Carell starred as Michael Scott in the [[NBC]] sitcom *The Office*, for which he won a Golden Globe Award. He was a correspondent on *The Daily Show with Jon Stewart* and later starred in films including *Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy* and *The 40-Year-Old Virgin*. His dramatic role as John du Pont in *Foxcatcher* earned him an Academy Award nomination for Best Actor. He also starred in the [[Netflix]] series *Space Force*.

American comedian, radio and television host. Harvey has hosted the game show [[Family Feud]] since 2010 and formerly hosted the [[Miss Universe]] competition. He began as a [[Stand-up comedy|stand-up comedian]] in the early 1980s and starred in the sitcom *The Steve Harvey Show*. His book *Act Like a Lady, Think Like a Man* (2009) was a bestseller, and he has won seven Daytime Emmy Awards.

Australian conservationist, zookeeper and television personality. Irwin achieved international fame through *The Crocodile Hunter*, a wildlife documentary series he co-hosted with his wife, Terri. The couple co-owned and operated Australia Zoo in [[Queensland]], which his parents founded. Irwin died from an injury caused by a stingray while filming an underwater documentary on the [[Great Barrier Reef]]. Numerous parks, zoos and streets, and a snail species, have been named in his honor.

American businessman, inventor and investor, and a pioneer of the [[Personal computer|personal computer]] revolution. Jobs co-founded [[Apple Inc.|Apple]] with [[Steve Wozniak]] in 1976 and helped bring the Apple II, one of the first highly successful mass-produced microcomputers, to market. After the board fired him in 1985, he founded NeXT and bought the computer graphics division of Lucasfilm, which became [[Pixar]]. He returned to Apple as chief executive in 1997, when the company was on the verge of bankruptcy, and oversaw products including the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad. The Macintosh 128K of 1984 was the first mass-produced computer with a [[User interface|graphical user interface]].

American comedian, actor, writer and musician. Martin became one of the most popular [[Stand-up comedy|stand-up comedians]] of the 1970s and was a frequent host of [[Saturday Night Live]]. He starred in films including *The Jerk* (1979), *Planes, Trains and Automobiles* (1987) and *Roxanne* (1987). He has won five [[Grammy Awards]], and in 2013 he received an honorary [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]]. With [[Martin Short]] he has toured since 2015, and the two co-starred with [[Selena Gomez]] in the Hulu series *Only Murders in the Building*.

American actor known as the "King of Cool." His antihero persona made him a top box-office draw from the late 1950s to the mid-1970s, in films including *The Magnificent Seven* (1960), *The Great Escape* (1963), *Bullitt* (1968) and *The Towering Inferno* (1974). He received an Academy Award nomination for *The Sand Pebbles* (1966) and became the world's highest-paid movie star in 1974. Diagnosed with terminal cancer, he went to [[Mexico]] for surgery against the advice of U.S. doctors. He checked into a hospital in [[Ciudad Juárez]] under a fake name and died of a heart attack a few hours after the operation.

Canadian former [[Basketball|basketball]] player and coach. Nash played 18 seasons in the [[National Basketball Association]], where he was an eight-time All-Star and a two-time Most Valuable Player (MVP). He ranks among the league's top players in career three-point shooting, free-throw shooting and assists. He was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2018, and from 2012 to 2019 he was general manager of the Canadian men's national basketball team.

American technology entrepreneur, electrical engineer and inventor. Wozniak co-founded [[Apple Inc.|Apple]] with [[Steve Jobs]] in 1976 and was the primary designer of the [[Apple II]], introduced in 1977 and one of the first highly successful mass-produced microcomputers. He had a major influence on the early concepts of the [[Mac (computer)|Macintosh]] from 1979 to 1981. After leaving Apple in 1985 he founded CL 9, which created the first programmable universal remote, released in 1987. He later focused largely on technology in K–12 schools, including a 1990 initiative to place computers in schools in the [[Soviet Union]]. He was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2000.

American actor, martial artist and producer. A 7th-dan black belt in aikido, Seagal began his adult life as a martial arts instructor in [[Japan]] and later taught aikido in [[Los Angeles]]. He starred in *Above the Law* (1988), regarded as the first American film to feature aikido in fight sequences, and in *Under Siege* (1992). Since 1991, multiple women have accused him of [[Sexual harassment|sexual harassment]] or assault. He is a supporter of the [[14th Dalai Lama]] and of [[Vladimir Putin]], backed the Russian annexation of Crimea in 2014, and was granted Russian citizenship in 2016.

American filmmaker, cinematographer and editor. A pioneer of modern independent cinema, Soderbergh made his breakthrough with *Sex, Lies, and Videotape* (1989), which won the Palme d'Or at the [[Cannes Film Festival]]. He won the Academy Award for Best Director for *Traffic* (2000), and his other films include *Erin Brockovich*, the *Ocean's* films and *Contagion*. Although his films often revolve around familiar concepts from big-budget Hollywood, he routinely employs an [[Avant-garde|avant-garde]] arthouse approach.

American filmmaker and producer, a major figure of the [[New Hollywood]] era and a pioneer of the modern blockbuster. Spielberg is the highest-grossing film director of all time, with films earning almost $11 billion worldwide. His films include *Jaws* (1975), *E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial* (1982), *Jurassic Park* (1993) and *Saving Private Ryan* (1998); *Schindler's List* (1993) and *Saving Private Ryan* both won him the Academy Award for Best Director. He collaborated with composer [[John Williams]] for decades and co-founded Amblin Entertainment and DreamWorks Pictures. Seven of his films have been inducted into the National Film Registry, and he has received three Academy Awards and twelve Emmy Awards.

American singer-songwriter, best known as a member of [[Fleetwood Mac]]. Nicks joined the band with Lindsey Buckingham in 1975, and its album *Rumours* won the Grammy Award for Album of the Year in 1978. She began her solo career in 1981 with *Bella Donna*, which topped the Billboard 200. Nicks is the first woman inducted twice into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]], as a member of Fleetwood Mac in 1998 and as a solo artist in 2019.

American [[Blues|blues]] guitarist and frontman of the trio Double Trouble. Vaughan became the leading figure of the 1980s blues revival with the debut album *Texas Flood*. He played guitar on [[David Bowie]]'s album *Let's Dance*. After struggling with alcoholism and drug addiction, he returned to touring in 1986 following rehabilitation. His album *In Step* included his only number-one hit, "Crossfire." He was killed in a helicopter crash in East Troy, Wisconsin, and an investigation concluded that pilot error caused the accident. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] posthumously in 2015.

American singer-songwriter, musician and record producer, blind since shortly after birth. Wonder signed with [[Motown]]'s Tamla label at age 11, and his single "Fingertips" topped the Billboard Hot 100 when he was 13, the youngest solo artist ever to top the chart. In the 1970s he made extensive use of [[Synthesizer|synthesizers]] on albums such as *Talking Book* (1972) and *Songs in the Key of Life* (1976), which helped reshape contemporary R&B. He has won 25 [[Grammy Awards]], the most by a male solo artist. In 1980 he campaigned to make [[Martin Luther King Jr.]]'s birthday a federal holiday, and he collaborated with [[Paul McCartney]] and [[Michael Jackson]] in the 1980s. He was conferred [[Ghana|Ghanaian]] citizenship in 2024.

Dish of solid food ingredients cooked slowly in liquid and served in the resulting gravy. Ingredients may include [[Vegetable|vegetables]] and meats such as beef, pork, rabbit, poultry and sausage, especially tougher cuts that become tender with slow, moist heat. Stews are simmered rather than boiled and are thickened by reduction, [[Flour|flour]] or starches such as [[Arrowroot|arrowroot]]. The oldest known evidence of stew was found in Japan, dating to around 5000 BC during the [[Jōmon period]]. Beef stew and dumplings were among England's national dishes in the 14th century, and regional examples include bouillabaisse, a fish stew from [[Provence]], and Brunswick stew from [[Virginia]].

Very simple drawing of a human or animal, with the limbs and torso drawn as straight lines and the head usually a circle. Stick figures appear in [[Prehistoric art|prehistoric art]], including cave paintings, and their roots are traced back over 30,000 years. They have been used as glyphs in logographic [[Writing|writing]] systems. Pictograms with stick figures were used at the 1964 Summer Olympics in [[Tokyo]] and the 1972 Summer Olympics in [[Munich]], and they became common in signage. After the [[World Wide Web]], stick figures were prominent in Flash [[Animation|animation]], and children often draw them.

Family of small ray-finned fishes, Gasterosteidae, with a Holarctic distribution in fresh, brackish and marine waters. Sticklebacks are carnivorous, feeding on small animals such as insects, crustaceans and fish larvae, and they are characterized by strong, isolated spines in their dorsal fins and usually no scales. The best-known species, the three-spined stickleback, reaches about 4 inches. Freshwater populations were trapped in [[Europe]], [[Asia]] and [[North America]] after the last Ice Age, 10,000–20,000 years ago, and they evolved features different from marine species. They were once thought related to [[Seahorse|seahorses]] but are now considered more closely related to eelpouts and sculpins. Males build nests from weeds held together with spiggin, a kidney secretion, and guard the eggs until they hatch 7–14 days later.

Resistance of an object to deformation in response to an applied [[Force|force]]; its inverse is flexibility or compliance. For a body with a single degree of freedom, stiffness is the force divided by the displacement it produces along the same direction, k = F/δ, usually defined under quasi-static conditions. In SI units it is measured in [[Newton (unit)|newtons]] per meter (N/m), while rotational stiffness is measured in newton-meters per [[Radian|radian]]. Stiffness is a property of a structure or component and depends on its physical dimensions, whereas the [[Elastic modulus|elastic modulus]] is a property of the constituent material. Shear and torsional stiffness are further measures.
